questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=3t-1,\,\,\,y=(t+5)(t-2),\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

The Cartesian equation of this curve is

$y=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=3t-1\,⇒\,t=\frac{x+1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=\frac{x+1}{3}$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(\frac{x+1}{3}+5)(\frac{x+1}{3}-2) \\  & =(\frac{x+1+15}{3})(\frac{x+1-6}{3}) \\  & =(\frac{x+16}{3})(\frac{x-5}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(x+16)(x-5).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=\sqrt{\,t+1\,},\,\,\,y=t(4-t),\,t\ge 0.
$$

The Cartesian equation of this curve is

$y=$
{{field-1}}$,\,x\ge 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\sqrt{\,t+1\,}\,⇒\,t={x}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t={x}^{2}-1$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =({x}^{2}-1)(4-({x}^{2}-1)) \\  & =({x}^{2}-1)(5-{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=({x}^{2}-1)(5-{x}^{2}).$

Finally, since $t\ge 0$ and $t={x}^{2}-1,$ we must have ${x}^{2}-1\ge 0,$ i.e., $x\ge 1.$

Therefore, the complete Cartesian equation is $y=({x}^{2}-1)(5-{x}^{2}),\,x\ge 1.$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x=\frac{t-5}{2},\,\,\,y=({t}^{2}-25)(t-4),\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{t-5}{2}\,⇒\,t=2x+5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=2x+5$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =((2x+5)^{2}-25)(2x+5-4) \\  & =(4{x}^{2}+20x+25-25)(2x+1) \\  & =(4{x}^{2}+20x)(2x+1) \\  & =4x(x+5)(2x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=4x(x+5)(2x+1).$

evidence.solution_quote: So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=4x(x+5)(2x+1).$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2t+5,\,\,\,y=(t-2)(t+1),\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

The Cartesian equation of this curve is

$y=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2t+5\,⇒\,t=\frac{x-5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=\frac{x-5}{2}$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(\frac{x-5}{2}-2)(\frac{x-5}{2}+1) \\  & =(\frac{x-5-4}{2})(\frac{x-5+2}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{x-9}{2})(\frac{x-3}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(x-9)(x-3).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x=\frac{1}{t+1},\,\,\,y=\frac{1}{t-2},\,t\ne -1,\,2.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{t+1}\,⇒\,t=\frac{1}{x}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now substituting $t=\frac{1}{x}-1$ into our expression for $y$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{((\frac{1}{x}-1)-2)} \\ y & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{x}-3)} \\ y & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1-3x}{x})} \\ y & =\frac{x}{1-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\frac{x}{1-3x}.$

Finally, since $t\ne -1,\,2$ and $x=\frac{1}{t+1},$ we must have $x\ne 0,\,\frac{1}{3}.$

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y=\frac{x}{1-3x},\,x\ne 0,\,\frac{1}{3}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Curve Defined Parametrically With Trigonometric Functions
questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\,\,y=\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,t\in (0,\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t=\frac{x}{2} \\ y=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sec}⁡t=y\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the Pythagorean identity ${sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1$ by ${cos}^{2}⁡t$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{{cos}^{2}⁡t}+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t}{{cos}^{2}⁡t} & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\ {(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t})}^{2}+1 & ={(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t})}^{2} \\ {tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{tan}⁡t=\frac{x}{2}$ and $\operatorname{sec}⁡t=y$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}+1={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is ${y}^{2}={(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}+1.$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=3\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,\,\,y=2\operatorname{csc}⁡t,\,0<t<\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The Cartesian equation of this curve is

$y=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=3\operatorname{cot}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cot}⁡t=\frac{x}{3} \\ y=2\operatorname{csc}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{csc}⁡t=\frac{y}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Pythagorean identity ${csc}^{2}⁡t=1+{cot}^{2}⁡t$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{csc}^{2}⁡t & =1+{cot}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We used here that $\operatorname{csc}⁡t>0$ and $\operatorname{cot}⁡t>0$ in the range $0<t<\frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, solving for $y$, we obtain

$$
y=2\sqrt{\,1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}\,}.
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the given curve is 
$y=2\sqrt{\,1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}\,}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\,\,y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The Cartesian equation of this curve is

$y=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t=-\frac{x}{4} \\ y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the double-angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡t=-\frac{x}{4}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{3} & =2{(-\frac{x}{4})}^{2}-1 \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\frac{2{x}^{2}}{16}-1 \\ y & =3(\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-1) \\ y & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{8}-3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\frac{3{x}^{2}}{8}-3.$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\,\,y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2} \\ y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using double angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{3} & =1-2{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2} \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\ y & =3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).$

evidence.solution_quote: So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+4,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The Cartesian equation of this curve is

{{field-1}}$=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t=\frac{x}{2} \\ y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+4\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=y-4\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Pythagorean identity ${sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-4)^{2}+{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x=2t^2, \,\,\, y=t^2+1, \quad t \geq 0.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t^2\mathbin{:}$

$$
x=2t^2 \quad \Rightarrow\quad  t^2 = \dfrac{x}{2}
$$

Now substituting $t^2=\dfrac{x}{2}$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={t}^{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{x}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x+1.$

Finally, since $t \geq0$ and $x=2t^2,$ we must have $x \geq 0.$

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y=\dfrac{1}{2}x+1, \quad x \geq 0 .
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Curve Defined Parametrically With Trigonometric Functions
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\csc{t},\,\,\, y=2\cot{t}, \quad 0 < t < \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{csc}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{csc}⁡t=x \\ y=2\operatorname{cot}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cot}⁡t=\frac{y}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the Pythagorean identity $\sin^{2}{t}+\cos^{2}{t}=1$ by $\sin^{2}{t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t}+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t} & =\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\ 1+{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t})}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t})}^{2} \\ 1+{cot}^{2}⁡t & ={csc}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\csc{t} = x$ and $\cot t =\dfrac{y}{2}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{(\frac{y}{2})}^{2} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ {y}^{2} & =4({x}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y^2 = 4\left( x^2-1 \right).$

Finally, since $0 < t < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\csc t,$ the interval on the $x$-axis is $x \geq 1.$
